EAST ASIA & PACIFIC ECONOMIC UPDATE | OCTOBER 2026 CHAPTER 2 55
Chapter 2. AI Adoption, Adaptation, and Advancement in
East Asia and Pacific
Artificial intelligence (AI) adoption is increasing across East Asia and Pacific among both individuals
and firms, though it remains below levels in advanced economies. Firms’ growing demand for AI-related
skills is often bundled with analytical skills, such as mathematics and critical thinking, and social skills,
such as communication and collaboration. AI innovation in East Asia, reflecting both adaptation and
advancement, is pivoting from Japan to China and the Republic of Korea. For most countries in the
region, adoption and adaptation of existing AI technology–especially of small AI tools—offer the main
pathway to reap AI benefits in the short term. Governments play a key role as enablers, users, and
regulators of AI. Efforts to improve the fundamental enablers of a conducive business environment, in
particular the availability and reliability of infrastructure and a skilled workforce, could yield double
dividends in harnessing AI for development and supporting broader growth momentum in East Asia and
Pacific. Policymakers can maximize AI benefits by ensuring digital foundations, by using AI to improve
the provision of public services, by strengthening institutional and regulatory readiness, and by deepening
intra-regional cooperation.
Introduction
Diffusion of AI. AI has emerged as a
general-purpose technology (GPT) promising
to reignite productivity growth and transform
production, jobs, and skills demand.
Ultimately, the development impact of AI
in emerging market and developing economies
(EMDEs) will depend on how it improves
productivity and the quality of jobs in
manufacturing, agriculture, and services as
well as public administration and social services
provision. The potential impact of AI has been
compared to the Industrial Revolution, but is
unfolding at ten times the speed (Rose 2025).
It took about 80 years for the steam engine
to reach lower-income countries, 40 years for
electricity, and 20 years for the internet. By
contrast, middle-income countries accounted
for half of ChatGPT’s global traffic within
six months of its launch (World Bank Group
2026b). In East Asia and Pacific, the use
of AI by individuals is currently increasing

Benefits of AI for EMDEs. The 2026 World
Development Report proposes a framework
to examine the implications of AI for
development. EMDEs can benefit from AI
in three steps: by adopting existing AI tools,
by adapting AI to local context and needs, and
by advancing the technology while building
their own frontier AI models alongside the
infrastructure needed to run them (World
Bank Group 2026b). Since each step requires
more investment, skills, and infrastructure than
the previous one, countries can participate in
the AI value chain in different ways. The
development of small AI solutions offers the
most cost-effective path to AI adaptation.
East Asia and Pacific in the AI value chain.
Several East Asian and Pacific countries
participate in the AI value chain, especially
in the upstream stages of the production
of semiconductors (chips) and access to
compute (that is, data centers), but less so
in the downstream stages of developing large
language models (LLMs).

still mostly confined to lower-value added
activities such as assembly, testing, and

• There has been a significant increase in
investments in data centers in several East

seven years (World Bank Group 2026a).
• While the development of large language

Focus of this chapter. While the influence
of AI is unmistakable in the region’s industrial
sector (as discussed in Chapter 1), the
realization of AI’s potential and its economic
impacts will depend on how firms and
individuals adopt, adapt, and advance this
technology across economic sectors. As
economies in East Asia and Pacific become
more service-oriented and AI is increasingly
embedded into production processes and
management practices, it will reshape product
and labor markets. This chapter examines the
following questions:
1. How is AI diffusing in EMDEs in East
Asia and Pacific?
2. How is AI affecting jobs and the demand
for skills in the region?
3. How is AI-related innovation distributed
in East Asia and Pacific?
4. What are the policies needed to fully
harness the potential of AI for the region’s
development?
Main findings
First, AI adoption remains nascent in most of
the region. AI adoption is increasing across
EMDEs in East Asia and Pacific both among
individuals and firms, but from a low base.
Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) use
by individuals living in emerging economies
in the region is well below the 33-percent
in advanced economies. Although work is
the largest use category, its work-related share
is lower than in other EMDEs. This is
consistent with the below-average 13-percent
share of workers in East Asia and Pacific in jobs
with predominantly non-routine, cognitive
(AI-complementary) tasks. In some countries
such as Thailand, only 12 percent of firms
report using any AI technology and 4 percent
pay a subscription for AI software or systems,
compared with 43 percent and 23 percent
in the United States, respectively. Low firm

viability: Thai firms report low expected

Based on the historical precedent of predictive
AI adoption, firms’ size, prior technological
capabilities, and proximity to AI knowledge
centers are key enablers of AI adoption.
Second, there is not yet a discernible impact on
AI-automatable jobs in EMDEs in East Asia
and Pacific, in contrast with emerging evidence
of negative impacts in advanced economies
and other EMDE regions. This is consistent
with the still nascent AI diffusion. AI-related
skills demand has grown in several EMDEs in
East Asia and Pacific, but remains below the
level of some advanced economies in the region
and other EMDEs. About 1 percent of online
job postings in EMDEs in the region require
AI-related skills, compared with 6 percent in
Singapore and 2–3 percent in Poland and India.
In China, demand for GenAI skills has risen
fast, especially after the release of DeepSeek,
but remains concentrated among listed,
larger, and more technologically advanced
firms. Analytical skills, such as mathematics
and critical thinking, and social skills, such
as communication and collaboration, are
emerging as AI-adjacent skills that are typically
bundled with the demand for AI-related skills.
Third, AI innovation, reflecting both adaptation
and advancement, is expanding rapidly
worldwide and even more rapidly in East
Asia and the Pacific. China, Japan, and the
Republic of Korea rank among the world’s
most prolific sources of AI patents, where
nearly half of patents originate in the past
five years, while the region’s other EMDEs
have barely entered the field. Although AI
innovation occurs in EMDEs in East Asia and
Pacific, it is increasingly owned by foreign
multinationals, builds mostly on U.S. and,

Fourth, efforts to improve the fundamentals
of a conducive business environment, in
particular the availability and reliability
of infrastructure and a workforce with
the right set of skills, could yield double
dividends in harnessing AI for development
and supporting broader growth momentum.
For most countries in the region, especially
Pacific islands, adoption and adaptation of
existing AI tools offer the main pathway to
reap AI benefits, but they are hindered by
weaknesses in institutional readiness, trusted
data ecosystems, digital foundations, and policy
implementation capacity. Beyond supporting
AI adoption and adaptation, strengthening
innovation ecosystems and data governance
would enhance the contribution of the more
developed economies in East Asia and Pacific
to AI advancement. Policymakers can also
maximize AI benefits by using it to improve
the provision of public services, providing
regulatory frameworks that foster public trust,
and deepening intra-regional cooperation

Contribution
First, this chapter provides new comparative
evidence on AI diffusion in EMDEs in East
Asia and Pacific, where uptake is advancing but
remains highly uneven. Population-normalized
usage data indicate strong individual use in
Malaysia, the Philippines, and Viet Nam,
but also show that connectivity constraints
continue to hinder population-wide adoption
in lower-income economies (Misra et al. 2025).
More broadly, gaps in connectivity, compute,
locally relevant data, and skills inhibit adoption
at scale (Arias et al. 2025; World Bank Group
2025). Yet comparable firm-level evidence
for EMDEs in East Asia and Pacific remains
scarce. This chapter uses new firm-level data
for some EMDEs in East Asia and Pacific
to compare AI adoption in the region with
advanced economies and other EMDEs.
Second, this chapter provides new evidence on
the skill bundles that can help workers thrive
in a labor market that is being disrupted by AI.
In advanced economies, AI has been associated
with large task-level productivity gains but
mixed employment effects, with adjustment
often taking the form of task and skill
reallocation (Brynjolfsson, Li, and Raymond
2025; Hampole et al. 2025; Humlum and
Vestergaard 2025), or adverse employment
effects in more AI-automatable jobs and
AI-intensive local labor markets (Bonfiglioli et
al. 2025; Calvino, Reijerink, and Samek 2025;
Huang et al. 2026). AI is associated with wage
premiums for AI skills and complementary
skills, but evidence from EMDEs in East Asia
and Pacific outside of China is limited (Fan,
Qi, and Leng 2026; Martins-Neto et al. 2026;
Stephany and Teutloff 2024). Using online
job posting data for a sample of EMDEs and
advanced economies, this chapter identifies
the demand for skill bundles that include AI,
domain-specific, analytical, and socioemotional
skills and compares this demand across multiple
countries in the region. The analysis of
AI-related skill bundles helps identify the
complementary capabilities workers would
need to benefit from AI rather than be displaced
by it (Cazzaniga et al. 2024).
Third, this chapter provides new comparative
evidence on AI innovation across East Asia
and Pacific, based on the AI patents filed and
identified using patent data and text analysis.
Comparable evidence on AI innovation in
EMDEs in the region remains scarce as the
literature has focused on documenting the
scale, ownership, and knowledge flows of
AI innovation in China, Europe, and the
United States (Fang et al. 2026; OECD 2025;
Santarlasci et al. 2025; World Intellectual
Property Organization 2019). The chapter
fills the gap by characterizing AI innovation in
East Asia and Pacific along four dimensions:
the geography of AI invention and how it
has been shifting within the region; the
divergence between where AI is invented
and who owns it; the sources of the knowledge
on which each economy’s AI builds; and the
role of human capital and public institutions
in generating innovation. Research on AI
innovation in EMDEs emphasizes diffusion
through trade and FDI (Fu 2020; Fu and
Shi 2022). The chapter complements this
research by documenting diffusion through
different channels, in particular, cross-border
collaboration and co-invention within
multinationals, and the knowledge flows
recorded in patent citations.
Data and Methodology
Data. Individual AI use is measured
using data from Anthropic and Microsoft
(annex 2.1). Firm AI use is measured
using data on adoption of machine learning
(“predictive AI”) from Spiceworks Ziff Davis

Aberdeen Group for 2016–22, online
recruitment platforms in China, and the World
Bank Enterprise Surveys in Thailand and the
United States. AI-exposure is measured using
indicators of the task intensity of occupations
from employment data from ILOSTAT and
labor force surveys for a sample of Southeast
Asian economies (Cambodia, Indonesia,
Malaysia, the Philippines, Thailand, Viet
Nam) and data from China’s economic census.
Demand for AI-related skills is measured
from millions of online job postings across
nine East Asia and Pacific economies, of
which five are EMDEs, and four comparator
economies between March 2025 and April
2026 (annex 2.2; Aedo et al. forthcoming).
AI innovation is measured using more than
100,000 AI patent applications filed through
the Patent Cooperation Treaty (PCT) between
2009 and 2024, drawn from the Autumn
2024 edition of PATSTAT and identified
following OECD (2025). The PCT is a system
managed by the World Intellectual Property
Organization (WIPO) through which a single
patent application can seek protection in
more than 150 member countries. Data on
STEM (science, technology, engineering, and
mathematics) graduates come from OECD
education statistics, official national sources,
and the UNESCO Institute for Statistics
(annex 2.3).
Estimation. The measurement of the task
intensity and AI-exposure of jobs follows Arias
et al. (2025) using the methodology of Autor
and Dorn (2013) and Felten, Raj, and Seamans
(2023). Online job-posting data are used to
identify AI-related skills alongside other digital,
technical and socio-emotional skills (annex
2.2). For each skill, the prevalence ratio is
computed by dividing the share of AI-related
job postings requiring that skill by the share
of all job postings that also require the skill.
A high ratio means the skill is distinctive
in AI recruitment–disproportionately
demanded relative to the average job posting.
Rarely demanded skills would score highly:
mathematics, for instance, is uncommon
overall but emerges as an AI-specific niche
skill. The analysis reveals emerging trends
and associations, not structural shifts or causal
effects of AI.
AI adoption
AI adoption is increasing across EMDEs in East
Asia and Pacific, both among individuals and
firms, but is still well below the global average.
In some countries, such as Thailand, low firm
adoption may reflect limited economic viability:
firms report low expected productivity gains from
AI, and high costs and insufficient knowledge
as barriers to AI use. Based on the historical
experience from the adoption of predictive AI
(machine learning tools), a firm’s size, prior
technological capabilities, and proximity to AI
knowledge centers are key enablers of AI adoption.
Individual use of GenAI
AI adoption. For most EMDEs in EAP ,
the largest gains are likely to come from the
broad adoption of existing AI tools while
adapting them to local needs (World Bank
Group 2026a). New data from Anthropic
and Microsoft’s Global AI Diffusion dataset
helps examine the utilization of Generative
Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) by individuals,
including for personal and work-related tasks.
This is important to more broadly assess
the potential impact of this technology.
Individual use for work captures task-level
utilization, which may occur without the
firm-level adoption that requires investments
and organizational changes to integrate GenAI
into a firm’s business process. Both individual
and firm-level uses of AI could change worker
and firm productivity.

Individual GenAI use is comparable to the
global average only in Viet Nam, Malaysia,
the Philippines, and China. According to
Anthropic, individuals in EMDEs in East
Asia and Pacific frequently use GenAI Claude
for coursework, which accounts for about
25 percent of AI uses—10–15 percentage

advanced economies (figure 2.3). Countries
with higher per capita incomes, a larger share
of the population with secondary education,
and wider internet use tend to use GenAI
more frequently. For instance, a 1 percent
higher GDP per capita is associated with a

10-percentage-point higher share of internet
users is associated with a 1 percent higher usage.
Individual GenAI Claude use for work.
Like in the rest of the world, individuals in
EMDEs in East Asia and Pacific use GenAI
most often for work (40 percent of AI queries).
GenAI use for work is positively correlated
with internet use and per capita GDP , similar
to overall GenAI adoption, whereas it is
not significantly correlated with the share of
secondary education attainment (figure 2.3).
Individual GenAI Claude use:
Augmentation and automation. According
to Anthropic, GenAI use can be broadly
categorized as promoting “automation” and
“augmentation,” depending on AI primarily
substituting or complementing humans in the
performance of tasks.
• In automation, AI performs a task largely
on behalf of the user with minimal human
intervention, such as responding to prompts
to format documents or generating an
output from a well-defined request.
• In augmentation, AI works alongside
the user through an iterative process, in
tasks such as developing ideas, supporting
learning through explanation of concepts,
or reviewing work through logic checks and
providing feedback and suggestions.

Lower per capita incomes are associated
with more frequent use of GenAI for task

Firms’ AI adoption. The World Bank
Enterprise Surveys (WBES) 2026 collected
data on the adoption of a range of AI
tools—including predictive, generative
and agentic AI—in six EMDEs, including
Thailand, and these are benchmarked against
the United States. The data reveal that AI
adoption and paid use is low among Thai
firms: only 12 percent report using any AI
technology and 4 percent pay a subscription
for AI software or systems, compared with 43
percent and 23 percent in the United States,
and 23 and 4 percent in India, respectively.
Uptake increased following the public launch
of ChatGPT on November 30, 2022 and, even
more prominently, around the public launch
of DeepSeek-R1 in January 2025 (figure 2.5).
Low adoption by Thai firms may reflect limited
economic viability: the expected benefits of
AI do not yet outweigh the costs of its adoption.

than in the United States may reflect lower
expectations of productivity gains from AI
adoption. The WBES survey asks firms
how much they expect sales per worker to

scenarios: rapid and slow AI development

Historical precedent: Predictive AI adoption
by firms. GenAI’s predecessor, machine
learning tools (hereafter “predictive AI”), has
been used in many settings to automate routine
workflows and improve predictive accuracy to
inform data-driven decision making. For
example, predictive AI has been used to
monitor transactions to detect fraud in finance
and optimize supply chain in manufacturing.
For 2016–22, establishment-level data on the
use of predictive AI is available for a sample
of 30,000 establishments of multinational
enterprises (MNEs), multi-plant firms, and
standalone firms across 31 countries, including
China and Thailand. Predictive AI was most
widely and most rapidly adopted in MNEs:
they—regardless of being headquartered in
advanced economies or EMDEs—were more
than twice as likely to adopt predictive AI than
domestic multi-plant firms, and five to six times
more likely than single-plant firms. China,
the EMDE that hosts the largest number of
multinational enterprise establishments in
manufacturing, is no exception to this pattern
(figure 2.6). A regression analysis using data on
all establishments of MNEs points to several
factors associated with greater adoption of
predictive AI:
• Prior technological capabilities of the
firm, measured by prior adoption of
enterprise resource planning (ERP) or
cloud computing;
• Proximity to AI knowledge centers ,
measured as the number of universities
and research centers with AI-intensive
publications during 2000–15 and that

Impact of AI on AI-automatable jobs.
Among AI-exposed jobs, the estimated impact
of AI has been most pronounced in occupations
that involve primarily routine cognitive tasks
in advanced economies, where automation
tends to be more economically viable because
of high labor cost. For example, the online
jobs platform Lightcast has data for hundreds
of millions of online job postings in advanced
economies and some Southeast Asian EMDEs
from the first quarter of 2018 to the second
quarter of 2025. Since the public release
of ChatGPT, the number of job postings in
advanced economies for occupations that rank
above-median in an index of automatability
by AI fell by an average of 5.8 percent relative
to occupations that rank below-median (figure
2.7; Huang et al. 2026). In the U.S., the
decline in AI-automatable jobs is concentrated
among entry-level and less-skilled jobs, and
in professional services and administrative
support occupations (Liu, Wang, and Yu 2025).
Applying the analysis of Huang et al. (2026)
in a sample of Southeast Asian EMDEs to data
from the same online platforms does not show
any discernible differential trend in online
job postings related to AI-automatability,
consistent with the lower AI adoption in these
countries.

jobs cannot be interpreted as causal because
the analysis does not fully account for other
confounding factors that affect the economy
and the labor market. There are several
measures of AI job exposure in the literature
which differ in terms of approaches and data
sources (for example, Demombynes, Langbein,
and Weber 2025; Eloundou et al. 2024;

However, the resulting measures are highly
correlated with one another (World Bank

measures is that they assume workers in
the same occupations perform similar
tasks in EMDEs and advanced economies.
However, using actual worker-level task data
from 47 EMDEs and advanced economies,
Lewandowski, Madoń, and Park (2026)
find that adjusting for within-occupation
differences in tasks halves average AI exposure
in the least-developed countries from 1 to 0.5
U.S. standard deviations (also refer to Gmyrek,
Viollaz and Winkler 2026).
Impact of AI on AI-exposed jobs through
trade. The diffusion of AI has also implications
for a country’s export-linked jobs. With the
rise of global value chains (GVCs), economies
increasingly specialize in tasks rather than
specific goods or services. In GVCs, production
is linked across multiple countries and sectors,
with each stage involving distinct tasks
performed by different workers and machines.
Through labor substitution and augmentation,
AI reduces the production costs for a given
output bundle and raises productivity, with
the magnitude of this productivity effect
increasing with the level of AI exposure.
Kruse and Yu (2026) combine recent labor
force surveys and input-output tables for
26 economies to measure export-linked jobs
across detailed occupations, classified as having
AI-augmentation potential, facing a risk of
AI substitution, or having low exposure.
In most EMDEs in the region, workers in
export-linked jobs have low exposure to AI and
are therefore neither at risk of AI substitution
nor likely to leverage AI to significantly boost
their productivity. In contrast, a larger share of
export-linked jobs is at risk of AI substitution
in higher-income economies, reflecting export
specializations in service sectors and more
routine-cognitive tasks within goods-producing
sectors.
Demand forAI-related skills
Significant demand for digital skills.
Realizing the potential of AI requires
equipping workers with digital skills as AI
tools are increasingly embedded in jobs.
Basic digital skills include transcribing texts
and using e-services, intermediate digital
skills include using accounting software and
designing web-based courses, and advanced
digital skills include machine learning and
designing cloud architecture. Online job
postings data reveal that demand for advanced
digital skills is concentrated in high-income
economies—especially Japan (36 percent),
Republic of Korea and Singapore (both 28
percent; figure 2.8). In Southeast Asian
EMDEs, like other peers, intermediate digital
skills account for about half of digital skill
requirements, followed by demand for basic
digital skills. Across all economies, advanced
digital skills are more often required in jobs
that involve non-routine cognitive and social
interaction tasks, while basic digital skills
requirements are more prevalent in routine
cognitive jobs.
Skills and position in the AI value
chain. The patterns of digital skill demand
reflect differences in economic structure
and an economy’s position in digital
technology-intensive global value chains (Aedo
et al. forthcoming):
• Advanced economies in East Asia and
Pacific. In the Republic of Korea,
the demand for advanced digital
skills is related to hardware-intensive
activities, reflecting their semiconductor
manufacturing and technology sectors,
while in Japan and Singapore, demand
focuses on platform and services-intensive
activities such as semiconductor
design, cloud computing, platform
management, and financial technology.

employers seek workers with specific skills, they
are not solely seeking technical qualifications
or credentials: they want a bundle of
complementary competencies. As digital
technologies automate routine tasks, employers
increasingly value bundles of complementary
technical, digital, and transversal (both
analytical and socio-emotional) skills required
for non-routine cognitive and interpersonal

Kahn 2018; Grundke et al. 2018; refer also to

skills by income level. Beyond these
common AI-adjacent transversal skills,
job postings for AI-related skills reflect
differences in the economies’ position

economies, like the Republic of Korea,

conduct academic research and to provide
expert advice, while in Southeast Asian
EMDEs employers stress AI-adjacent skills
to engage with stakeholders like clients and
team members, as illustrated, for example,
by the Philippines (figure 2.11).

AI innovation
AI innovation, reflecting both adaptation and
advancement, is increasing rapidly worldwide.
China, Japan, and the Republic of Korea rank
among the world’s most prolific sources of AI
patents, while the region’s EMDEs remain at
an earlier stage of AI patenting. Although
some AI innovation occurs in EMDEs in East
Asia and Pacific, it is increasingly owned by
foreign multinationals, builds mostly on U.S.
and, increasingly, Chinese knowledge, and relies
disproportionately on public institutions.
Rise of AI patenting. Patented AI innovation
has accelerated sharply over the past decade.
This can reflect new AI tools resulting from
local adaptation to develop AI solutions as
well as advancement of AI frontier models.
The number of AI patents filed under the
Patent Cooperation Treaty (PCT) more than
quadrupled between 2009–16 and 2017–24.
AI patenting rose even faster than overall
patenting: the share of AI patents in all patent
applications filed under the Patent Cooperation
Treaty increased from just over 1 percent in
2009–16 to almost 5 percent in 2017–24
(figure 2.12). Innovation is thus not merely
expanding but orienting toward AI, consistent
with its role as a general-purpose technology.
Shift toward more advanced AI tools. The
composition of AI patenting has changed as its
scale increases. In 2009–16, computer-vision
applications and traditional machine-learning
techniques accounted for about two-thirds of

more advanced techniques: deep-learning
patents rose from about 8 percent to
26 percent, and machine learning to 39
percent, while computer vision fell to 15
percent (figure 2.12). Frontier techniques
such as generative foundation models and
general AI grew from 1 to 7 percent over

A concentrated and shifting geography of
innovation. AI patents remain heavily and
increasingly concentrated in a few particularly
innovative economies. The phenomenon of
concentration of the AI value chain discussed
in World Bank Group (2026b) is perhaps
even more prominent when looking at the
AI patenting activity. Inventors residing in
the United States and China together account
for more than half of AI filings in recent
years. In 2021–24, U.S. inventors accounted
for 29 percent of AI patents filed under the
Patent Cooperation Treaty, while the share
invented by Chinese inventors rose from
about 22 percent in 2013–16 to about 26
percent in 2021–24 (figure 2.12). In East Asia
and Pacific, the composition of AI patents is
shifting towards inventors in the Republic of
Korea’s and China as the share of Japanese
inventors is declining. Inventors in Southeast
Asian economies accounted for only 1 percent
of global patents, a very small share but still
three times that of other emerging economies
in Latin America, at 0.3 percent.
Divergent ownership of inventions. Each
patent records two different pieces of
geographical information: inventors and
applicants. Inventors are the researchers who
created the invention and applicants are the
entities, commonly firms and institutions,
that file the patent and hold the resulting
property rights. Inventors’ locations therefore
show where the innovation is carried out,
while applicant location shows who owns
the innovation. The two coincide when a
domestic entity patents the work of its own
researchers, but they diverge when an entity
owns inventions created by research teams
abroad. The divergence can be measured
as the difference between each economy’s
share among applicants and its share among
inventors on AI patent applications under the
Patent Cooperation Treaty in 2021–24 (figure
2.12). The United States appears more often as
an owner than as an inventor, and so do Japan,

EAST ASIA & PACIFIC ECONOMIC UPDATE | OCTOBER 2026 CHAPTER 2 71
the Republic of Korea, and Singapore. But
China shows the opposite pattern: Chinese
researchers invent more AI than Chinese
applicants own, consistent with evidence that
multinational-sponsored patents account for
a significant share of international patents by
China-based inventors (Branstetter, Li, and
Veloso 2015). This divergence is starkest
in the region’s developing economies: a
substantial and growing share of AI invested
in Southeast Asia is owned by foreign entities,
rising from roughly one-fifth in 2009–16 to
about one-third in 2017–24, predominantly
held by U.S. entities (annex 2.3)
The ownership-invention gap concentrates
in frontier AI technologies. The gap between
patent ownership and invention was broadly
uniform across AI subfield applications during
2009–16 for both the U.S. and China,
except in Artificial General Intelligence (AGI)
development. By 2017–24, the gap in both
countries narrowed and became concentrated
in the frontier applications: GenAI, machine
learning, and deep learning (figure 2.12E). The
United States held the largest ownership share
in these frontier fields in the earlier period, but
China’s ownership share rose sharply and now
exceeds that of the United States in AGI, Gen
AI and deep learning (figure 2.12).
United States as the largest source of AI
knowledge. For nearly every economy, the
knowledge used in their AI patents comes
primarily from technologies invented in the
United States: patents invented in ASEAN
and the EU27 draw the largest share of
their citations from the U.S. patent stock,
and even Chinese-invented AI patents drew
more on U.S. than on Chinese patents in the
earlier period. But China’s knowledge base
is turning inward. The share of citations by
Chinese-invented AI patents that go to other
Chinese patents rose from about one-third
in 2009–16 to about half in 2017–24,
indicating that Chinese AI increasingly builds
on a maturing domestic knowledge stock
alongside knowledge from global frontier.
Chinese-generated knowledge is also becoming
a more important source for other economies,
whose citations of the Chinese patent stock
have risen over the same period (annex 2.3).
Importance of talent for innovation.
Across economies, more STEM graduates are
associated with more AI patents (figure 2.13).1
But the departure from the fitted line shows
that China and the United States combine
the world’s largest STEM graduate pools with
exceptionally large AI patent output, while
Japan and Republic of Korea convert moderate
graduate bases into disproportionately large AI
patenting. India sits far below the fitted line,
producing one of the world’s largest STEM
graduate pools while patenting little AI, and
Malaysia shows a similar shortfall in East Asia
and Pacific. These gaps may partly reflect
that STEM graduates in these economies
produce patents attributed elsewhere, either
graduates migrated or are working within
foreign multinational enterprises in their home
country—both patterns are consistent with
the ownership evidence documented above.
This suggests that leveraging graduates into
frontier invention requires complementary
capabilities—such as research institutions,
firms in the technological frontier, and access
to global AI knowledge—that some economies
with large STEM talent pools lack.
The public-private mix in innovation. More
than 70 percent of AI patents arise from firms’
research and development activities in every
country, but the exceptions are concentrated in
East Asia and Pacific (figure 2.13). Companies
account for about 95 percent of AI patents
filed under the Patent Cooperation Treaty and

Universities, public research institutes, and
government agencies play a larger role in
ASEAN economies, accounting for over 20
percent of patents, compared to about 17
percent in Republic of Korea and 14 percent
in China. A larger public role can reflect
a solid research ecosystem, such as China’s
academy system and the Republic of Korea’s
research institutes (Fang et al. 2026; World
Intellectual Property Organization 2019).
However, in emerging economies, it can also
signal underdeveloped capital markets and
insufficient protection of intellectual property
rights, which hinder the ability and incentives
of domestic firms to adapt and advance AI tools.
Policy implications
Realizing AI’s potential for development depends
on a broad set of policy reforms to support AI
adoption, adaptation, and advancement, with
governments playing a key role as enablers, users,
and regulators of AI (World Bank Group 2026b).
Efforts to improve fundamental enablers, in
particular a conducive business environment,
adequate infrastructure and financing, and a
skilled workforce, could yield double dividends
in supporting growth and harnessing AI for
development. Other complementary policies are
examined in previous regional studies (refer to
Arias et al. 2025; De Nicola et al. 2025; World
Bank Group 2024, 2026a). Policy priorities
differ across countries in the region because
the gaps and market and policy failures that
inhibit these fundamentals vary across contexts
and development stages. In most EMDEs in the
region, the adoption and adaptation of existing AI
technology—especially of small AI tools—offer the
main pathway to reap AI benefits. Policymakers
can maximize AI benefits by ensuring digital
foundations, by using AI to improve the provision
of public services, by strengthening institutional
and regulatory readiness, and by deepening
intra-regional cooperation.
Infrastructure
Access to basic physical and digital
infrastructure. While countries in East Asia
and Pacific have improved the availability of
physical and digital infrastructure in the last
decades, important differences remain both
across and within countries. Across countries,
in 2024, internet penetration rates vary from
98 percent and 91 percent for Malaysia and
Thailand to 19 and 35 percent for Papua
New Guinea and Timor-Leste (World Bank
Group 2026a). Within countries, internet
adoption rates remain significantly higher
among better-educated, higher-income, and
urban households and firms (World Bank
Group 2024).
Access to compute. The number of data
centers in the East Asia and Pacific region,
including those with AI capacity, has grown
substantially in the last 10 years, especially
in China, Indonesia, and Malaysia (box 2.1).

EAST ASIA & PACIFIC ECONOMIC UPDATE | OCTOBER 2026 CHAPTER 2 73
BOX 2.1 Data Centers in East Asia and Pacific
The adoption, adaptation, or advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) requires access to “compute”, the
ability to process large amounts of data. Local data centers offer one form of access to compute. High-capacity
and reliable energy grids in some EMDEs in East Asia and Pacific make them attractive data center locations.
Data center investment is also attracted by other good fundamentals, such as sound governance and regulatory
quality, and a skilled workforce. Efforts to improve these fundamentals are therefore likely to constitute
“no-regrets” policies that benefit data center investment as well as broader investment.
Introduction
Data centers in East Asia and Pacific. Demand
for cloud computing has risen sharply as
digitalization continues and the adoption of
AI tools becomes increasingly widespread among
firms and consumers. Cloud compute can be
accessed globally or locally in local data centers.
While EMDEs in East Asia and Pacific lag behind
advanced economies in the intensity of data
centers, the number of data centers has grown
rapidly in the several East Asian countries over
the past ten years (figure B2.1.1). China accounts
for the largest share of new data centers and
Indonesia, Malaysia, and Thailand explain the
majority of the remaining growth. Malaysia and
Thailand are among the top 10 recipient countries
worldwide of data center investment, together
with other EMDEs like Brazil and India (World
Bank Group 2026a)
The case for local data centers. Local data
centers are needed for frontier AI applications,
but for many forms of AI adoption are not
required. But countries increasingly seek local
or regional compute capacity for purposes
of data sovereignty, cybersecurity, regulatory
compliance, digital resilience, and support for
public-sector and enterprise AI deployments.
The vast majority of existing data center capacity
offers conventional cloud services: data storage
and processing, software, and website hosting.
This box was prepared by Jonah Rexer, Jonathan Timmis, and
Margaret Triyana (DECPA).
Indeed, in East Asia and Pacific, some AI-driven
applications—such as Google searches, video calls,
and cloud storage—can be run using data centers
in Europe or the Americas. More sophisticated AI
applications—such as robotics and autonomous
driving—require low latency (the delay between
a user’s request and the system’s response) and,
therefore, proximity to high-capacity data centers
(figure B2.1.1). If adoption of such more
sophisticated applications grows in the more
advanced digital economies in the region, or
for data sovereignty purposes, demand will also
grow for secure data centers locally or in close
proximity. Other drivers of rising demand for
local infrastructure are also the search for greater
digital resilience, and the support for public-sector
AI deployments.
Focus of this box. By enabling productivity
gains, including from AI applications, data center
investments can potentially support downstream
economic activity and the creation of more
productive, high-skilled jobs (World Bank Group
2026b; FTI forthcoming). Moreover, data centers
construction involves the creation of jobs, and
their maintenance require highly-skilled workers.
However, complementary factors—including a
skilled workforce, a reliable and affordable energy
supply, and robust governance—are needed to
reap these benefits by ensuring the infrastructure
is used productively. Moreover, because of their
intensive resource use, these investments raise
environmental concerns. This box examines the
enabling factors of data center investments by
considering the following questions:

infrastructure investment does not keep pace with
demand (Chandramowli et al. 2024; Bogmans et
al. 2025).
Future evolution of the energy mix. The
AI industry is exploring ways to mitigate the
pressure on energy and water systems created
by data centers (World Bank Group 2026a).
Several data center operators are working on

Global compute capacity. Since 2022, when
OpenAI’s public release of ChatGPT inaugurated

from 111,000 NVIDIA H100 equivalents
annually to 1.9 million in 2025, or a 17-fold
increase in AI computing power. This dramatic

and most planned AI compute has yet to come
online (figure B2.1.1). Despite the recent fast
expansion in data centers in East Asia and Pacific
and other EMDEs, most of the world’s installed
capacity is in the United States and China, which
also remain the dominant developers of new AI
models.

The role of fundamentals. Data center
investment is attracted by good fundamentals:
high quality infrastructure such as a reliable
energy grid and water supply, sound governance
and regulatory quality, and a skilled workforce.
These are all factors that are also important
for productivity-enhancing investment more
broadly. Efforts to improve these fundamentals
are therefore essential and likely to constitute
“no-regrets” policies that benefit data center
investment as well as broader investment,
especially if the marginal investment is funded by
data centers themselves.
Fundamentals in East Asia and Pacific. While
several economies in East Asia and Pacific are

been in some instances binding constraints for
the construction of data centers. Projects
have been delayed due to insufficient investment

connections to energy grids, and the challenges of
coordinating across multiple government agencies
(World Bank Group 2026a). Malaysia’s Green

have also deterred data-intensive trade,
functioning as a non-tariff barrier on

an opportunity for East Asian economies.

an opportunity to increase energy supply,

Financing
Access to finance. One of the main factors
cited by East Asian firms as an impediment
to AI adoption is its cost (figures 2.5). This
calls for facilitating access to finance specifically
designed to support AI technology adoption,
especially for micro, small, and medium-sized
enterprises (MSMEs). Advanced economies in
the region show a path that other countries
can follow. The Republic of Korea, for
instance, introduced the “AX Sprint Preferential
Track” in 2026, specifically designed to
accelerate financing for companies pursuing AI
transformation, as part of its SME Policy Fund.
In Japan, the “IT Introduction Subsidy” has
now been rebranded—as the “Digitalization
& AI Introduction Subsidy”—to emphasize
AI. In Singapore, the 2026 budget expanded
the Productivity Solutions Grant to support a
wider range of digital and AI-enabled solutions.
Supporting AI adoption, adaptation
and advancement
Prioritizing adoption and adaptation of
small AI applications to local context. Most
EMDEs can reap the benefits from AI by
adopting and adapting AI tools developed
elsewhere (World Bank Group 2026b). For
many well-defined tasks, small AI applications
derived from open-weight models are more
cost-effective and can match the functionalities
of general-purpose frontier models (Quách
and Huang 2026). Because the weights are
public and the model is already trained–the
most expensive part–governments or firms only
need to pay for the adaptation to local languages
and data at a fraction of the cost (World Bank
Group 2026a). AI Singapore’s SEA-LION
pre-trains multilingual models across 13
regional languages. Thailand’s ThaiLLM,
Vietnam’s VinaLLaMA, Indonesia’s Cendol and
the Philippines’ FiLLM are examples of locally
adapted models to local languages and data. In
Indonesia, Bahasa-first chatbots are serving the
population through business and government
services in ways that English-only tools never
could. In Viet Nam, an AI coach tailored
to Vietnamese speakers has become one of
the country’s most popular language-learning
tools, while AI-powered medical imaging
systems are helping under-resourced hospitals
improve diagnoses. Governments can
catalyze such local adaptation initiatives by
strengthening digital foundations—including
high-quality, interoperable data in local
languages and domains, trusted transactions,
digital identity, and credentials—and by
leveraging public procurement and digital
government modernization.
Small AI in EAP can support jobs. Several
countries in the region are already pursuing
adoption and adaptation of small AI tools
to improve business, social services, and
jobs. In the Philippines, AI is enabling
better irrigation and access to finance for
smallholder rice farmers by leveraging satellite
crop-health data and improved credit-scoring,
and AI-powered forecasting tools are helping
rural homestays and boutique hotels manage
the deep occupancy slumps that monsoon
season brings. In Viet Nam, AI-powered tools
are helping small hotels and tour operators
generate promotional visuals and dynamic
pricing at much lower cost. Physical AI is
being deployed in elderly care in Australia and
Japan, where therapeutic robots have helped
reduce loneliness and anxiety among dementia
patients by augmenting rather than displacing
care workers (Eggleston et al. 2026; Wang,
Shen, and Chen 2022).

example, public procurement contracts with
access to government data led to Chinese firms
developing new commercial software (Beraja et
al. 2023).
Positioning along the AI value chain.
Countries need not participate in every stage
of the AI value chain to benefit from AI.
Advanced chips, large-scale compute, and
frontier AI models are highly concentrated and
require investments and capabilities beyond
most developing economies. Opportunities
also vary along the value chain. China
already participates across much of the
AI value chain, including semiconductors,
compute, AI models, and applications.
In EMDEs in East Asia and the Pacific,
selected upstream activities—such as
semiconductor manufacturing and, where
conditions are favorable, data centers—can
complement larger gains from adapting and
developing AI applications. Moving into
higher-value AI activities requires gradual
capability building. Countries can sequence
investments by sector while strengthening the
skills, research capacity, firm capabilities,
and knowledge links needed to adopt,
adapt, and eventually advance AI. Strategic
dependence can be reduced through diversified
suppliers, interoperability, strong knowledge
partnerships, and safeguards for sensitive data
and critical infrastructure (World Bank Group
2026b).
The role of the public sector
In addition to implementing policy to
ensure the above fundamental enablers of
AI, governments can leverage AI’s potential as
users and as regulators of AI, while guarding
against AI’s risks (World Bank Group 2026b).
Governments can also enact policies aimed at
increasing consumers’ protections and promote
intra-regional cooperation.
Governments as AI users: public
procurement. Public procurement can play
an important role in supporting adoption and
adaptation, including by creating opportunities
for local solution providers where local
language, data, and institutional context
matter. Thailand, for instance, is pursuing
procurement reforms intended to expand
opportunities for startups and innovative
suppliers to participate in government
markets and position public procurement
as a tool to support innovation and economic
transformation. While these reforms remain
at an early stage and evidence of large-scale AI
procurement is still limited, they illustrate how
governments can use demand-side policies to
encourage development and adoption of locally
adapted digital and AI solutions.
Governments as AI users: provision of
public services. Countries in East Asia can
benefit from AI also by using it to improve
the provision of public services. Advanced

economies provide successful examples. The
OneService Chatbot in Singapore, for instance,
enables residents to report municipal issues
through a simple interactive online interface.
The chatbot processes more than 30,000
cases each month, automating key tasks such
as extracting case details, predicting issue
categories, and routing cases to the appropriate
agencies. This saved an estimated 2,000 man
hours each month and reduces resolution times
by up to two working days. Another example
comes from the Republic of Korea, where the
national water utility has deployed predictive
AI across more than 40 water treatment
plants, including for energy management
and predictive equipment maintenance. These
positive examples also highlight the importance
of putting in place the right safeguards, which
typically include clear legal authority, human
oversight for consequential decisions, audit
trails, independent review, and accessible
channels to challenge automated decisions.
Governments as AI regulators. As regulators,
governments help establish the institutional
conditions for digital trust through robust data
governance, trusted data-sharing arrangements,
and effective safeguards for privacy, security,
and responsible use. The World Development
Report 2026 argues that the most effective
approach to AI regulation is iterative:
policymakers can begin by assessing the
regulatory landscape and identifying gaps, then
design policy instruments, build enforcement
and compliance capacities, and continuously
monitor and adapt (World Bank Group
2026b). Following the EU’s landmark AI
Act of 2024, several countries have enacted
horizontal AI laws, including Japan, the
Republic of Korea, and Viet Nam. Other
countries, such as China, are following a more
“risk-scenario-by-risk-scenario” approach to
AI regulation. While different contexts are
better served by different approaches, sound
AI regulation is an important determinant of
AI adoption. Because regulatory uncertainty
remains a significant impediment to AI
adoption and adaptation, effective governance
frameworks will also need to address bias
and fairness, data privacy and security, and
the transparency of automated decisions
(including their accountability). Existing
frameworks—including those on data
protection, consumer protection, cybersecurity,
competition, and non-discrimination—may
already address many AI-related risks, but
their effectiveness will depend on adequate
institutional and regulatory capacity and
implementation. Digital foundations—such
as digital identity, digital public infrastructure,
and verifiable credentials—can help speed AI
adoption. Getting these frameworks right
matters beyond compliance: public trust in AI
is a prerequisite for sustained adoption, and
early signs of backlash in advanced economies,
discussed in Chapter one, suggest that trust
cannot be taken for granted.
Governments’ role in ensuring online safety
and cybersecurity. Large-scale, cross-border
scam-center operations have emerged in
parts of East Asia and Pacific, where fraud
schemes are targeting victims worldwide
through telecommunications networks,
payment platforms, and money-laundering
channels (UNODC 2025). AI is making these
operations cheaper, more scalable, and more
convincing. Tools like deepfake impersonation,
multilingual phishing, synthetic identities,
and automated social engineering allow
scammers to target victims across languages
and geographies. The financially and
digitally vulnerable are particularly exposed,
as they may struggle to avoid scams or
absorb resulting losses. Addressing this
problem requires digital and financial literacy
programs, accessible complaint channels,
mechanisms for rapid fund recovery, and
clearer responsibilities for financial institutions,
payment providers, telecommunications
companies, and digital platforms in
detecting and disrupting AI-enabled fraud.
